reconcile.connective: Gill reads 1 Corinthians 13:7's 'believeth all things' as charity toward persons' characters, not the credulity about words and spirits the other texts warn against.

discrepancy.connective: Steve Wells's Skeptics Annotated Bible presses these five verses as flatly incompatible answers to whether we should believe everything, not different senses of 'believe.'

skeptic.name: Steve Wells
skeptic.attribution: Steve Wells, The Skeptic's Annotated Bible, "Should We Believe Everything?" (skepticsannotatedbible.com, est. 1999; print ed. SAB Books, 2013)

excerpts.excerpt_text: though such a man will not believe every spirit, every preacher and teacher, nor any but such as agree with the Scriptures of truth, the standard of faith and practice; nor will he believe every word of man, which is the character of a weak and foolish man; indeed, a man of charity or love is willing to believe all the good things reported of men; he is very credulous of such things, and is unwilling to believe ill reports of persons, or any ill of men; unless it is open and glaring, and is well supported, and there is full evidence of it; he is very incredulous in this respect:
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Gill's exposition of 1 Cor 13:7 explicitly distinguishes the 'believeth all things' of love (charitable belief in good reports of persons) from believing 'every spirit' or 'every word of man' -- echoing 1 John 4:1's and Proverbs 14:15's own vocabulary -- directly resolving the tension the question raises.

pd_work.resource: John Gill, Exposition of the Entire Bible (1746-63)
pd_work.author: John Gill
pd_work.note: Gill treats 1 Corinthians 13:7 directly, distinguishing love's charitable 'believeth all things' toward persons from the credulity about words, spirits, and reports that Proverbs 14:15, 1 Thessalonians 5:21, and 1 John 4:1 warn against -- the same passage anchoring this row's reconcile pole; Haley's Alleged Discrepancies could not be confirmed (full-text search) to treat this credulity/testing cluster at all.
